narrative:
The model estimated a 54.9% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is only slightly above a coin flip, but because it crossed the school’s risk cutoff, your application was denied. This is a risk estimate, not a judgment that you cannot succeed.

The strongest influence was your third-year class-rank decile. At 6, it was a bit above the accepted-student average of about 5.79, and this factor actually pushed the prediction toward passing. However, two other factors outweighed it. Your LSAT score of 32.50 was below the accepted-student average of 37.18 and was the next most important factor, pushing toward failure. Your first-year class-rank decile of 4 was also below the accepted average of 6 and pushed toward failure. In combination, the model saw weaker standardized-test performance and a lower early academic rank as the main reasons for elevated bar-exam risk.

To move forward, request a human review of the denial and ask whether the prediction can be reconsidered alongside context not captured in the data. Consider retaking the LSAT after preparation, and provide evidence of academic improvement or strong third-year performance. You may also ask admissions what conditions or supplemental materials could support a future application or conditional admission.
